transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-05-15
Time: 10:30 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Rachel (Redwood CSM), Liam (Aurora Head of Platform), Priya (Aurora SRE), Jordan (Data Scientist), Evan (Engineer)

[00:00] Maya Chen: okay everyone good morning thanks for joining this is our weekly poc sync i'm Maya from Redwood, i'll let diego take point on the technical incident follow-up but we'll do quick context and then dive in
[00:12] Diego Alvarez: hey team, quick agenda: re-run of the 5/12 incident timeline, logs that priya shared, hypotheses, quick mitigations we can apply today, and then bench plan. sound good?
[00:22] Priya Singh: yes that's perfect. i pushed a trimmed set of logs to the shared folder, note the kube events around 11:05 had a flurry of throttled API calls too, and we saw pods restart after liveness probe failures
[00:36] Liam O'Neill: to add, our traffic spike was legitimate — end of month settlement jobs kicked off at 11:00 and some customers retried, so we saw bursty traffic for ~7 minutes
[00:48] Diego Alvarez: ok that matches. so i pulled the trace samples: there are two things happening in parallel — upstream rate-limits from our side hitting the Redwood API, and then client retries without jitter causing retry storms, which in turn produced elevated p99 latency and some 5xx responses from the model serving cluster
[01:10] Jordan Park: i've got a question — some of our queued requests show duplicate inference calls. could that be due to retries being attempted before the initial request reached the model?
[01:20] Diego Alvarez: yeah that can happen. if the client (or a proxy) triggers an immediate retry on a connection timeout, it can create duplicated work. combined with batching this can blow memory and kv cache usage and then cause OOMs or 5xxs downstream
[01:36] Evan Miller: on our side we had Nginx proxy with default timeouts, we didn't have a centralized retry policy. i think our client library was doing naive retries on 408/timeout and 5xx
[01:48] Maya Chen: totally understandable, we see this pattern a lot. for a short term mitigation we recommend three levers: 1) client-side exponential backoff with full jitter, 2) a modest circuit-breaker threshold so you stop retrying into a strained backend, and 3) adjust proxy timeouts to ensure the initial request gets enough time (and align with Redwood SLOs)
[02:12] Priya Singh: can you share exact numbers? like initial delay, max retries — we need something we can paste into our helm values
[02:20] Diego Alvarez: sure. start with initial backoff 200ms, factor 2, max jitter, max retries 3 for 4xx/429, and for 5xx/timeouts max retries 2 with longer base (500ms). combine with a circuit breaker that opens after 5 consecutive errors for 30s. we'll send a snippet. 
[02:39] Liam O'Neill: what about idempotency — some of these calls can't be retried safely because they create state in our system
[02:46] Maya Chen: good call — we recommend marking idempotent vs non-idempotent at the client layer. non-idempotent should either not be retried, or retried only with server side dedupe tokens. also you can set a short TTL on those tokens.
[03:00] Jordan Park: related — our batch sizes are small right now, maybe 8 tokens per batch, could increasing batching reduce thundering or make it worse?
[03:09] Diego Alvarez: depends. increasing batching reduces per-token overhead so it's cost-effective and often reduces overall throughput pressure, but it also increases request latency. for a spike scenario batching can help smooth load if you have steady arrival rate; for sudden bursts it can add latency and bigger memory pressure. we can test.
[03:27] Priya Singh: earlier logs show a KV cache thrash. is that from variation in sequence lengths?
[03:33] Diego Alvarez: likely — lots of short interactive requests mixed with long settlement docs will cause inefficient kv cache locality. tuning the caching policy (shorter kv residency for long runs) or routing long jobs to a dedicated model variant can help
[03:46] Evan Miller: what about rate limits — we saw 429s from Redwood and some 503s. are the 503s internal saturation?
[03:54] Maya Chen: yes, 429s are being returned by the Redwood API gateway when request rate exceeds your configured quota or burst window. 503s generally indicate internal saturation on the serving runtime (e.g., insufficient worker threads or OOM). in this case our telemetry shows worker queue growth and then rapid restarts for a subset of workers during the spike
[04:14] Liam O'Neill: how quickly can we get dedicated capacity? if we had a reserved pool would this be prevented?
[04:20] Maya Chen: Dedicated capacity reduces noisy neighbor risk and gives predictable throughput. it isn't an instant switch but we can provision a small dedicated pool for the pilot within 48–72 hours subject to contract. it would mitigate the internal saturation class of 503s but you still need client retry hygiene to avoid retry storms
[04:36] Diego Alvarez: long term options we discussed: dedicated pools, model quantization/variants for high-throughput jobs, and smarter routing (e.g., route long settlement jobs to batch-optimized variant). for immediate triage we'll focus on client retries, proxy timeouts and a short circuit breaker
[04:52] Priya Singh: i'd like to see an example of how to set the Redwood SDK retries vs our proxy. we have two layers of retries today which is not great
[04:59] Diego Alvarez: yes avoid retry-on-retry. recommended architecture: have the client set conservative retries and let the proxy be retry-naive off (or vice versa). we prefer single coordinated retry layer. i'll include a config sample for both environments (nginx + k8s liveness/readiness adjustments)
[05:16] Jordan Park: do you have any suggestions for observability? we had trouble correlating request ids across layers
[05:23] Rachel Park: on our side we surface token-level cost breakdown and per-request trace IDs if you pass the request-id header. also we can add tracing hooks to your observability backend (we've integrated with datadog and honeycomb) so you can follow the request across the gateway and serving runtime
[05:37] Evan Miller: perfect, we'll start passing a request-id.
[05:40] Diego Alvarez: next i want to walk through the specific incidents from 11:02-11:09 on 5/12. i pulled CPU and memory graphs — you can see at 11:03 p99 jumps and then worker restarts at 11:05
[05:54] Priya Singh: that's what we saw, the liveness probe threshold was pretty aggressive. we increased the periodSeconds after the incident but i'll share the original config
[06:04] Maya Chen: good to hear you relaxed it; aggressive liveness checks on warmup can exacerbate restarts during spikes. other quick wins: increase readiness probe window and ensure warmup endpoints don't trigger heavy init work
[06:18] Liam O'Neill: one ask from our security team — they want the SOC2 and network diagrams and also any info on encryption at rest for caches
[06:27] Rachel Park: noted — i'll share our SOC2 summary and the high level network diagram. charlie from trust & safety also confirmed our KV cache uses AES-256 and integrates with KMS for key rotation; i'll include the compliance FAQ
[06:41] Priya Singh: thanks. back to mitigation: what about rate-limit tuning? can we increase burst window temporarily for settlement windows?
[06:48] Maya Chen: yes the gateway has adjustable burst and sustained rate settings per API key. we can increase the burst by a factor for your pilot day and then monitor. but raising bursts without retry controls could move the problem into internal saturation, so do both together
[07:02] Diego Alvarez: propose small experiment: for next settlement window, increase gateway burst by 2x, set client retry to 3 with jitter, enable circuit breaker (5 errors open 30s), and run a 30 minute synthetic bench that reproduces end-of-month load. Diego + Evan will run bench, Maya will provision temporary burst increase, Priya will collect logs
[07:22] Jordan Park: what metrics should we look at to validate success?
[07:26] Diego Alvarez: p99 latency, 5xx per minute, worker restart count, queue depth, and rate of duplicated inferences. also track cost per inference if batching changes
[07:36] Maya Chen: i'll drop a short runbook in the shared folder with the exact metrics and thresholds for pass/fail
[07:43] Liam O'Neill: ok good. any discussion on longer term — rollover to dedicated if we see consistent high throughput?
[07:50] Maya Chen: yes, if bench shows stable behavior we can talk committed reserved capacity; Redwood dedicated gives you predictable throughput and isolation which prevents internal saturation from other customers
[07:59] Priya Singh: timeline question — after we run bench and share logs, how fast can you turn around a config snippet and changes?
[08:06] Diego Alvarez: config snippet same day (today/tomorrow), circuit breaker example by Monday, and we can provision burst increase within 24 hours after you sign off on test window
[08:16] Rachel Park: i'll also attach the SOC2 and KMS notes by end of day tomorrow
[08:21] Evan Miller: i'll coordinate with Priya on the bench scripts; we have a jmeter profile we can adapt
[08:26] Jordan Park: small note — can we enable model variant fallback so long jobs don't use the interactive variant?
[08:32] Maya Chen: yes, we can add a routing rule to send requests with >2k token context to a batch-optimized variant or quantized variant. that is slightly more involved (model registry pinning) but doable during pilot
[08:44] Diego Alvarez: quick recap of action items and owners, i'll send the retry and circuit breaker snippets; priya will share logs and configs; evan will run bench; maya/rachel will share docs and provision temporary burst; then we regroup after bench.
[08:59] Liam O'Neill: thanks everyone, that covers it for us. appreciate the clear next steps
[09:03] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with artifacts and schedule the bench. speak soon

Meeting end.
